name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
short_description: Dramatic 61-acre park built on a former gypsum quarry with waterfalls, a grotto, and a Roman temple on a rocky island

beats.script_body: Beneath the pleasant lawns of Buttes-Chaumont lies a history of medieval horror. In the Middle Ages, as far to the west as Place du Colonel-Fabien, this land was the site of the gibbet of Montfaucon — established by Saint Louis (1223–70) as a sign of royal justice over the city. It was an elaborate stone structure with some 16 columns, each ten meters high. From it literally scores of decaying criminals' bodies could be hanging at any time. The gibbet was a place of execution in its own right, but also the place of exhibition of the remains of individuals tortured and executed in one of the many execution sites in Paris. Bodies could be left there for two or three years or more, at the end of which time, crows and — in bad times — wolves having done their worst — they were a gruesome sight, and their noisome stench wafted towards the Faubourg du Temple. In its garbage dump years, this landscape also fed a plump army of rats, who could strip a corpse to its skeleton within 24 hours.

fact_check.notes: Claim attributed to Colin Jones, Paris: The Biography of a City — footnoted in source.

beats.script_body: Monsieur Alphand had his work cut out for him when Haussmann and Napoleon III directed him to transform the foul terrain in eastern Paris into a scenic garden that would become Buttes-Chaumont. Some visitors are aware that in an earlier life the park served as a quarry for gypsum — plaster of Paris — as well as a garbage dump. But the genius landscape engineer and architect pulled off an inspired metamorphosis: today Buttes-Chaumont is one of the city's most popular parks, where sprawling and picnicking on the grass is permitted to weekending crowds from all over the city.

beats.script_body: Wandering the three miles of walking paths at Buttes-Chaumont — up and down the gentle hills beneath the cedars of Lebanon, past a grotto with a waterfall — you'll come to a lake with a huge rock above it, which in turn is topped by a mock Corinthian temple. There are good views of Montmartre and Saint-Denis from up here. You can cross the lake on a suspension bridge or on the Pont des Suicides.

beats.script_body: The popular Rosa Bonheur restaurant and guinguette — open for dancing, eating, and drinking Wednesday through Sunday until midnight, even when the park is closed — is named for Rosa Bonheur (1822–1899), the most famous female French painter of the nineteenth century. Her painting The Horse Fair hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. She was scorned in her day for wearing pants, smoking cigarettes, and enjoying the company of women.

beats.script_body: The robust and exuberant Julia Child, early in her time as a Parisian, found her way to Buttes-Chaumont on foot with her husband Paul: "Paris was wonderfully walkable. . . . one could easily hike from the Place de la Concorde to the top of Montmartre in a half-hour. . . . One cold afternoon just before New Year's, Paul and I strolled up to the Buttes-Chaumont park. At the top of the hill, by the little Greek temple, we looked back at Sacré-Coeur on Montmartre, now silhouetted through layers of mist by the declining sun." Then they retired to a nearby cozy bistro, complete with cats, dogs, neighborhood characters, and two monkeys squealing and chattering.

physical_cues.cue: The hilltop with the little Greek/Corinthian temple, looking back toward Sacré-Coeur on Montmartre

beats.script_body: In the streets bordering the park today, there are a number of ethnic bistros and cafes, including L'Estampe at 74, rue de Botzaris. In the picturesque Mouzaia District — named for a place in Algeria — between Buttes-Chaumont and Square de la Butte-du-Chapeau-Rouge, in the streets around rue Miguel-Hidalgo and rue de Mouzaia, you can wander the pedestrian cobbled streets of terraced villas and small gardens of fruit trees and flowers, perhaps en route to the Danube metro.

name: Pere Lachaise Cemetery
short_description: World's most visited cemetery with over 3 million annual visitors and graves of Chopin, Jim Morrison, Oscar Wilde, and Edith Piaf

beats.script_body: Colette (1873–1954), ecstatic lover of nature, would approve mightily of her final resting place. There are twelve thousand trees in Père-Lachaise Cemetery, avenues of cypresses, sycamores, tall, ancient chestnuts, a thick sheltering green roof over the cemetery's 105 acres of unspoiled beauty. Flowers are planted around the graves, some garlanding the monuments, symbolizing perpetual affection for the dead. "Throughout my existence," Colette wrote not long before she died, "I have studied flowering more than any other manifestation of life. It is there, for me, that the essential drama resides, and not in death, which is just a banal defeat."

beats.script_body: Among the 300,000 men and women buried in Paris's largest cemetery are icons of a prodigious flowering of French civilization — writers, painters, sculptors, singers, composers, and cineastes who make us love life more. You can stroll the silent hillsides, follow the long winding cobbled paths, stirred to your depths as you suddenly come upon the graves of Proust and Wilde, Delescluze, Daumier, and Poulenc. Memory, said Gertrude Stein: the only true immortality. Her grave is at the eastern edge of avenue Circulaire.

beats.source_passage: Among the 300,000 men and women buried in Paris's largest cemetery are icons of a prodigious flowering of French civilization who inspired a cultural reverence for that flowering in science, philosophy, politics, and especially the arts—the writers, painters, sculptors, singers, composers, and cineastes who make us love life more. Time spent in Pere-Lachaise quickens that love. There's no hurry here, no distractions. You can stroll the silent hillsides, follow the long, winding cobbled paths, stirred to your depths as you suddenly come upon the graves of Proust and Wilde, Delescluze, Daumier, and Poulenc. You can stop midway at a bench along a steep avenue to contemplate this landscape of memory. Memory, said Gertrude Stein: the only true immortality. (Her grave is at the eastern edge of avenue Circulaire?)

beats.script_body: From the heights of Père-Lachaise you can trace a remarkable cluster of nineteenth-century genius on your map. Chopin lies down the hill near the center, not far from Colette, or from another of George Sand's lovers, Alfred de Musset. Delacroix, buried under black lava to the west, was the romantic painter's version of his beloved Chopin's romantic music — his artistic style a striving for a surprising violent exotic beauty. Balzac, another friend of Delacroix and another genius of that great nineteenth-century artistic explosion, rests in the same section.

beats.script_body: In the vicinity of Colette's flower-strewn black granite grave are the lovers Héloïse (1101–1164) and Abélard (1079–1142), together in death in eternal defiance of the ecclesiastical powers that forced them apart in life. Their bodies were moved into Père-Lachaise — along with Molière and La Fontaine — in an effort to attract the important dead to what was a remote section of Paris when the cemetery was opened by Napoleon in 1804.

beats.script_body: In the seventeenth century the land of what is now Père-Lachaise had belonged to the Jesuits, who called it Mont Louis. The prominent Jesuit Francis de la Chaise d'Aix, confessor to Louis XIV, lived here and retired to a splendid country house on Mont Louis. Supposedly, the simpatico confessor and the young king-to-be watched the civil revolt called the Fronde (1649–1652) from here — "the hill of Charonne" — that traumatic vigil the source of the Sun King's lifelong fear and hatred of the mob, the frondeurs, which would eventually drive him to abandon Paris and move the royal court to Versailles.

beats.script_body: Two hundred years after Louis XIV's Fronde vigil, the Paris Communards made their last stand here among the tombstones — and in the nearby streets of Ménilmontant, Charonne, and Belleville. Finally subdued on May 28, 1871, 147 rebels were rounded up and shot against the eastern perimeter wall; the corpses of another thousand Communards were dumped in pits against the same wall. Today the Mur des Fédérés — the Wall of the Communards — to the right and down a few steps off avenue Circulaire — is a site of annual pilgrimage to commemorate the bravery of the working classes and the savagery of a government terrified of popular revolt. Now classified as a national historical monument, the Wall is always decorated with the flowers and wreaths left by pilgrims who arrive in all seasons.

Finally subdued on May 28, 1871, 147 rebels were rounded up and shot against the eastern perimeter wall; the corpses of another thousand Communards were dumped in pits against the same wall. Now classified as a national historical monument, the Wall is always decorated with the flowers and wreaths left by pilgrims who arrive in all seasons.

beats.script_body: The Dutch filmmaker Heddy Honigmann's documentary Forever unfolds an elegiac profile of the consoling beauty of Père-Lachaise. Some last words of Colette's resonate with the film's muted joy: "What a wonderful life I've had. I only wish I'd realized it sooner."

opening_hours_basis: A gated walled cemetery with closing bells; hours follow the City of Paris's published summer pattern (opens 08:00 weekdays, 08:30 Sat, 09:00 Sun, closing 18:00).
visit_basis: Vast hillside cemetery with cobbled avenues and many famous graves to hunt down over a wide area; an outdoor walk with no building to enter.
judgement_basis: A hushed cemetery of hard cobbled lanes where loud running children draw disapproval, though its quiet benches suit low conversation; it is gated and locked at nightfall so nobody can be left standing inside.
queue_basis: Entry is through free open gates with no ticket desk or security screening, so visitors walk straight in without waiting.

anchors.label: The Mur des Fédérés
anchors.basis: The Communards' wall is a fifty-metre stretch of the cemetery's own eastern boundary in division 76, reached down a few steps off the avenue Circulaire, and the memorials to the deported stand directly opposite it across that alley — the corpus beat says so and Julien gives the pair twenty unbroken minutes as ONE place (06-resident-novelty-seeker.md). Forty metres from the middle of the wall covers the strip of flowers and wreaths in front of it and the memorials facing it, and stops short of the graves eighty metres north. Placed by hand from the wall's own published position, never derived from the cemetery pin 316 m away.

anchors.label: Edith Piaf's grave
anchors.basis: The most visited grave in the cemetery, in division 97 among the memorials to the Resistants — the corpus beat places her beside them, and that corner is about eighty metres north of the Communards' wall. Thirty-five metres covers the plot and the gravel path people stand on to look at it, and does not reach the wall's own chapter.

anchors.label: Oscar Wilde's tomb
anchors.basis: Epstein's winged figure stands alone on the avenue Carette in division 89, a quarter of a kilometre north of the Communards' wall — far enough that nobody at the wall hears it by accident, which is what Julien's ordering asks for. Thirty-five metres covers the avenue in front of the monument, where a person stands back far enough to see the whole of it, and the rows either side.

anchors.label: The columbarium
anchors.basis: The crematorium and its columbarium corridors sit just north-east of the main rond-point, and the corpus beat directs the visitor along the first corridor of the lower level; a person stands in the forecourt between the pavilions to take the building in before going down. Forty metres round the forecourt covers the entrances to the corridors and stops well short of the Piaf and Wilde anchors further east.

anchors.label: Balzac and Nerval
anchors.basis: Balzac's column with the bronze bust by David d'Angers stands in division 48 on the Chemin des Acacias loop, and the corpus's own text places Nerval directly opposite it — one standing position serves both: a person stands on the path between the two graves and turns. Thirty metres covers both plots and the path.

anchors.label: Delacroix's tomb
anchors.basis: The black Volvic-stone sarcophagus in division 49, a short walk along from Balzac; a person stands on the path before it to look at the austere Roman form. Twenty-five metres is the plot and the path, clear of the Balzac position.

anchors.label: Allan Kardec's dolmen
anchors.basis: The flower-covered dolmen in division 44 draws a standing crowd of its own; a person stands at the railing among the tributes to read the inscription the beat quotes. Twenty-five metres holds the plot and the gathering space in front of it.

anchors.label: Rossini's cenotaph
anchors.basis: The cenotaph stands on the Avenue Principale a short way up from the main entrance; a person stands on the avenue itself to look at it. Twenty-five metres spans the avenue and the plot without reaching the entrance gates.

anchors.label: The Monument aux Morts
anchors.basis: Bartholome's memorial fills the hillside where the Avenue Principale meets the grand steps; a person stands back on the avenue to take the carved procession in. The corpus places Bartholome's own tomb nearby and David's heart on the second set of steps, so forty metres round the monument covers all three as one standing position; Géricault's tomb in division 12 adjoins the same carrefour — the walk reads Bartholomé, the Monument and Géricault standing in one place.

anchors.label: Cino del Duca's Pieta
anchors.basis: The Messina Pieta with its standing Virgin is in the divisions north-east of the crematorium; a person stands before the white marble group to see why the pose is unusual. Twenty-five metres is the plot and its path, clear of the columbarium forecourt.

name: Parc de la Villette

beats.script_body: The huge Cité des Sciences et de l'Industrie, like a number of the other buildings at La Villette, rises above abandoned abattoirs: La Villette was originally the site of the city's main slaughterhouse. The park goes on and on for miles, past one innovative themed garden after another — the Garden of Mirrors, of Dunes, of Winds, of Shadows, of Dragons (with a dragon slide) — all joined together by the Promenade des Jardins. Other highlights near the southern entrance include the Conservatoire de Paris, the Musée de la Musique with five floors of instruments, and the Cité de la Musique auditorium.

opening_hours_basis: A large open urban park that is freely walkable and not enclosed by closing gates, so not gated.
visit_basis: Very large modern park with canal, lawns, themed gardens and the red follies spread over a big area; crossing and exploring it usefully absorbs around 45 min, all outdoors.
judgement_basis: This very large park has vast traffic-free lawns and open ground where children can run freely, ample benches and lawn edges quiet enough to talk, and unusually for Paris it stays open and lit at night with people and venues about, so it passes all three.
queue_basis: A large open urban park with multiple unbarred entrances and no ticket or bag check, so there is no line to enter the grounds.

name: Parc de Belleville

beats.script_body: Walk from boulevard de Belleville, the bustling, gritty hub of artists, students, and immigrant residents from the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, up the hill of rue de Belleville — no. 72 is the legendary birthplace of Edith Piaf — then turn right into rue Piaf, and keep climbing. Bear right at the top toward the park's welcoming panorama: a higher overview of Paris than from Montmartre. Descending the steep paths and steps, beneath arches of wisteria, you'll come into the lower park meadow, unforgettable in June when the roses are in bloom.

name: Jardin Naturel

beats.script_body: A few steps from the Réunion exit from the cemetery, the city created this nature reserve as an educational resource for neighborhood schoolchildren who study the ecosystem here. There are woods, a pond with water lilies, fish, dragonflies, frogs, all sorts of insects. With two hundred varieties of plants and singing birds fluttering through woods dense with laurel and spirea, this is a man-made haven for nature lovers and people watchers.

name: Cemetery of Eglise Saint-Germain de Charonne

beats.poi_name: Cemetery of Eglise Saint-Germain de Charonne
beats.script_body: From place Gambetta, walk down rue Stendhal and descend the staircase alongside pretty houses; from the square in front of the fifteenth-century church — though the first church on this site dates from the ninth century — you will see the entrance to the cemetery, a bucolic sanctuary on a hill of cherry trees in April as well as flowering shrubbery. You're in the ancient village of Charonne, still a countryside-within-the-city.
